title: Symmetrical Faults
description: Short-circuit currents of three-phase faults: DC offset, subtransient and transient reactances, Thévenin and Z-bus methods, fault levels and breaker ratings.

study.title: Faults
study.body: A **fault** is an unintended short circuit, usually an insulator flashover caused by lightning, wind, ice, trees or animals. On overhead lines single line-to-ground faults are by far the most common, while **balanced three-phase faults** are rare (a few per cent) but often give the largest currents. Being balanced, a three-phase fault is solved with the familiar per-phase circuit. Fault currents set the ratings of circuit breakers and the settings of protection relays.

study.title: Explore: the DC offset
study.body: Closing a sinusoidal source onto an $R$–$L$ circuit (or a fault occurring) gives a steady AC current plus a decaying **DC offset**, with time constant $T = L/R = X/(\omega R)$. In the worst case the offset equals the AC peak, and the first current peak nearly doubles. The rms of the asymmetrical current is $K(\tau)$ times the symmetrical value, with $\tau$ in cycles. Drag $X/R$: high-$X/R$ circuits (near generators) keep their offset for many cycles.

study.title: Synchronous machine reactances
Three-phase fault calculation
study.body: Replace the network seen from the fault point by its **Thévenin equivalent**: the prefault voltage $V_F$ (often taken as 1.0 pu, neglecting load currents) behind $Z_{th}$, built with the machines' subtransient reactances. The fault current in amperes uses the current base of the zone where the fault is. With prefault load, add the load currents by **superposition**: fault-only currents plus prefault currents.

study.title: The bus impedance matrix
study.body: $\mathbf Z_{bus} = \mathbf Y_{bus}^{-1}$ (machines included as shunt reactances) gives the Thévenin impedance of **every** bus at once: $Z_{nn}$. For a bolted fault at bus $n$ with prefault voltage $V_F$ everywhere, the fault current and the voltage at every other bus $k$ during the fault follow directly; branch currents follow from those voltages.

study.title: Short-circuit MVA
study.body: The **fault level** of a bus is $S_{sc} = \sqrt3\,V_{nom}I''_F$. With $V_F$ = 1 pu it equals $S_{base}/|Z_{th,pu}|$, so a utility supply is often specified only by its fault level: its Thévenin impedance is $V^2/S_{sc}$. A strong bus (high $S_{sc}$) holds its voltage well but demands breakers with a high interrupting rating; series reactors are used to limit fault levels.

study.title: Circuit breakers
study.body: A breaker must carry the first-cycle (momentary) current and then **interrupt** the fault at a current zero after its contacts part, typically 2–5 cycles after fault inception. Ratings are stated as rms **symmetrical** current at rated voltage; standards (ANSI/IEEE C37) build in an allowance for DC offset up to $X/R$ ≈ 15, so then the simple $E/X$ fault current can be compared with the rating. Near large generators $X/R$ is higher and the asymmetry factor $K(\tau)$ at contact parting must be taken into account.

study.title: Worked example: fault at the end of a line
study.body:
100-MVA base: generator $X''$ = 0.20 pu, transformer 0.10 pu, 138-kV line 0.10 pu; bolted fault at the far end with $V_F$ = 1.0 pu.
- $Z_{th}$ = j(0.20 + 0.10 + 0.10) = j0.40 pu, so $I''_F$ = 1/0.40 = 2.5 pu.
- At the fault (138-kV zone, $I_{base}$ = 418 A): 2.5 × 418 = 1.05 kA.
- In the generator (13.8-kV zone, $I_{base}$ = 4.18 kA): 2.5 × 4.18 = 10.5 kA.
- Fault level at the line end: 100 MVA/0.40 = 250 MVA.

steps.title: Three-phase faults
steps.body: A fault short-circuits phases to each other or to ground. A **bolted three-phase fault** is rare but severe, and it is **balanced**, so it is solved per phase with Thévenin's theorem. Its current sets breaker ratings.

steps.prompt: Because a three-phase fault is balanced, its currents can be found from a single per-phase circuit.
steps.explanation: All three phases see the same impedances and are shorted together symmetrically, so the currents form a balanced set: solve phase a and shift by ±120°. Unbalanced faults (line-to-ground, line-to-line) need symmetrical components.

steps.title: The DC offset
steps.body: Fault current in an $R$–$L$ circuit = steady AC component + a decaying **DC offset** whose size depends on the point on the voltage wave at which the fault occurs. In the worst case (below, $X/R$ = 10) the first peak almost doubles. The offset decays with $T = L/R = X/(\omega R)$.

steps.prompt: A fault occurs in a {{f}}-Hz circuit with $X/R$ = {{XR}}. Find the time constant of the DC offset.
The symmetrical fault current is {{Iac|A}} (rms) and $X/R$ = {{XR}}. Find the rms asymmetrical current {{tau}} cycles after the fault, assuming the maximum DC offset.
steps.explanation: $K = \sqrt{1 + 2e^{-4\pi\tau/(X/R)}}$ = $\sqrt{1 + 2e^{-4\pi\times{{tau}}/{{XR}}}}$ = {{sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))||3}}. $I_{rms}$ = {{sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))||3}} × {{Iac|A}} = {{Iac*sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))|A}}.

steps.prompt: Drag $X/R$ until the DC offset (dashed) has decayed to 1/e ≈ 37 % of its initial value after {{N}} cycles.
steps.explanation: The offset falls to 1/e after one time constant, so $T$ = {{N}} cycles = {{N}}/$f$. Since $T = (X/R)/(2\pi f)$: $X/R = 2\pi$ × {{N}} = {{2*pi*N}}. Transmission circuits have $X/R$ around 10–20; near large generators it can exceed 40.

steps.title: Subtransient, transient, synchronous
steps.body: At a generator's terminals the AC fault current itself decays: limited first by the **subtransient** reactance $X''_d$, after a few cycles by the **transient** reactance $X'_d$, and finally by the synchronous reactance $X_d$. The graph is for $X''_d$ = 0.15, $X'_d$ = 0.25, $X_d$ = 1.5 pu with $E$ = 1.0 pu (log time axis).

steps.prompt: An unloaded {{S|VA}}, {{V|V}} generator with $X''_d$ = {{X}} pu at rated voltage suffers a bolted three-phase fault at its terminals. Find the subtransient fault current.
The steady-state three-phase short-circuit current of a generator can be smaller than its rated current.
steps.explanation: With $E$ ≈ 1.0 pu and $X_d$ ≈ 1–2 pu, the sustained fault current $E/X_d$ is about 0.5–1 pu. That is why protection must act on the large subtransient and transient currents and why a sustained fault current alone is a poor fault indicator. (Field forcing by the exciter raises $E$ somewhat.)

steps.title: Thévenin at the fault
steps.body: Seen from the fault, the network is a Thévenin source: prefault voltage $V_F$ (usually 1.0 pu) behind $Z_{th}$, with generators represented by $X''_d$. Then $I''_F = V_F/Z_{th}$ in per unit; multiply by the current base **of the faulted zone** to get amperes.

steps.prompt: On a 100-MVA base, a generator ($X''$ = {{Xg}} pu) feeds a {{VH|V}} line ({{Xl}} pu) through a transformer ({{Xt}} pu). A bolted three-phase fault occurs at the far end of the line. Find the fault current in amperes ($V_F$ = 1.0 pu).
steps.explanation: $Z_{th}$ = j({{Xg}} + {{Xt}} + {{Xl}}) = j{{Xg+Xt+Xl}} pu, $I''_F$ = 1/{{Xg+Xt+Xl}} = {{1/(Xg+Xt+Xl)}} pu. At the fault (line zone) $I_{base}$ = 100 MVA/(√3 × {{VH|V}}) = {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*VH)|A}}, so $I''_F$ = {{1/(Xg+Xt+Xl)*1e8/(sqrt(3)*VH)|A}}.

steps.prompt: Same system: 13.8-kV generator, $X''$ = {{Xg}} pu, transformer {{Xt}} pu, {{VH|V}} line {{Xl}} pu, fault at the line end (100 MVA, $V_F$ = 1.0). What current flows in the **generator**?
steps.explanation: The per-unit fault current, {{I}} pu, is the same in every zone; only the base changes. In the 13.8-kV zone $I_{base}$ = 100 MVA/(√3 × 13.8 kV) = {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}, so the generator carries {{I*1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}. The {{I*1e8/(sqrt(3)*VH)|A}} option is the line-side current.

steps.title: Fault level
steps.body: The **short-circuit MVA** (fault level) of a bus is $\sqrt3V_{nom}I''_F$. With $V_F$ = 1 pu it equals $S_{base}/|Z_{th}|$, so a fault level fully describes a source's Thévenin impedance, $V^2/S_{sc}$.

steps.prompt: The Thévenin impedance at a bus is j{{Z}} pu on a 100-MVA base. Find its fault level.
steps.explanation: $S_{sc} = S_{base}/|Z_{th}|$ = 100 MVA/{{Z}} = {{1e8/Z|VA}}: the bolted fault current is {{1/Z}} pu at 1.0 pu voltage.

steps.prompt: A utility specifies its {{V|V}} supply point only by a fault level of {{Ssc|VA}}. Find the Thévenin reactance per phase in ohms.
steps.explanation: $Z_{th} = V^2/S_{sc}$ = ({{V|V}})²/{{Ssc|VA}} = {{V^2/Ssc|Ω}} (line-to-line voltage and three-phase MVA, like $Z_{base}$). The fault current would be {{Ssc/(sqrt(3)*V)|A}}.

steps.prompt: A 13.8-kV bus is fed by the utility (fault level {{Ssc|VA}}) and by a local {{S|VA}} generator with $X''$ = {{X}} pu. Find the three-phase fault current at the bus ($V_F$ = 1.0 pu, 100-MVA base).
steps.explanation: Utility: $Z$ = 100/{{Ssc/1e6}} = {{Zu}} pu. Generator on 100 MVA: {{X}} × 100/{{S/1e6}} = {{Zg}} pu. The two sources are in parallel at the bus, so their currents add: 1/{{Zu}} + 1/{{Zg}} = {{1/Zu + 1/Zg}} pu × {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}} = {{(1/Zu + 1/Zg)*1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}.

steps.prompt: Inserting a series reactor between a bus and its supply lowers the fault level at the bus.
steps.explanation: The reactor adds to $Z_{th}$, so $S_{sc} = S_{base}/|Z_{th}|$ and the fault current fall. Current-limiting reactors let cheaper breakers be used, at the cost of extra voltage drop and reactive losses in normal operation.

steps.title: Faults with Z-bus
steps.body: Invert $\mathbf Y_{bus}$ (with the machines' $X''$ as shunt branches to the reference) to get $\mathbf Z_{bus}$. A fault at bus $n$ draws $I''_F = V_F/Z_{nn}$, and the other bus voltages drop to $E_k = (1 - Z_{kn}/Z_{nn})V_F$. One matrix covers faults at every bus.

steps.prompt: Two generators, $X''$ = j{{X1}} pu at bus 1 and j{{X2}} pu at bus 2, are joined by a line of j{{X12}} pu. Prefault voltages are 1.0 pu, load currents neglected.

ask.explanation: With det $= Y_{11}Y_{22} - Y_{12}^2$ = {{det}}, the off-diagonal element is $Z_{12} = -Y_{12}/\det$ = (1/{{X12}})/{{det}} = {{Z12||4}} pu.

steps.prompt: Two generators, $X''$ = j{{X1}} pu at bus 1 and j{{X2}} pu at bus 2, are joined by a line of j{{X12}} pu. Prefault voltages are 1.0 pu, load currents neglected. A bolted three-phase fault occurs at bus 2.

ask.prompt: Find the fault current in per unit.
Find the voltage at bus 1 during the fault, in per unit.
Find the current in the line from bus 1 to bus 2 during the fault, in per unit.
ask.explanation: Bus 2 is at 0 and bus 1 at $E_1 = 1 - Z_{12}/Z_{22}$ = {{1 - Z12/Z22}} pu, so $I_{12} = E_1/X_{12}$ = {{(1 - Z12/Z22)/X12|pu}}. The rest of the fault current, {{1/Z22 - (1 - Z12/Z22)/X12|pu}}, comes from generator 2.

steps.prompt: Bus 4 of a 100-MVA study has $Z_{44}$ = j{{Zt}} pu and a nominal voltage of {{V|V}}. Find its fault level.
steps.explanation: $S_{sc} = S_{base}/|Z_{44}|$ = 100 MVA/{{Zt}} = {{1e8/Zt|VA}}, i.e. a fault current of {{1/Zt}} pu = {{1e8/Zt/(sqrt(3)*V)|A}} at {{V|V}}.

steps.prompt: Near a large generator, a fault gives {{I|A}} symmetrical with $X/R$ = {{XR}}. The breaker's contacts part {{tau}} cycles after the fault. Find the rms asymmetrical current at contact parting (maximum offset).
steps.explanation: $K(\tau) = \sqrt{1 + 2e^{-4\pi\tau/(X/R)}}$ = $\sqrt{1 + 2e^{-4\pi\times{{tau}}/{{XR}}}}$ = {{sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))||3}}. $I$ = {{sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))||3}} × {{I|A}} = {{I*sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))|A}}. The frequency does not matter when time is counted in cycles.

steps.prompt: A 138-kV bus has a fault level of {{Ssc|VA}} and $X/R$ below 15. Which of these standard interrupting ratings is the smallest one that is adequate?
steps.explanation: $I''_F = S_{sc}/(\sqrt3V)$ = {{Ssc|VA}}/(1.732 × 138 kV) = {{If|A}}. With $X/R$ ≤ 15 the symmetrical $E/X$ current can be compared directly with the symmetrical interrupting rating: pick the smallest rating above {{If|A}}.

steps.prompt: A bus has $Z_{th}$ = j{{Zt}} pu (100 MVA). A series reactor of j{{Xr}} pu is added between the bus and its supply. By what percentage does the fault level at the bus fall?
steps.explanation: $S_{sc} \propto 1/|Z_{th}|$: before 100/{{Zt}} = {{1e8/Zt|VA}}, after 100/{{Zt+Xr}} = {{1e8/(Zt+Xr)|VA}}. Reduction: 1 − {{Zt}}/{{Zt+Xr}} = {{100*(1 - Zt/(Zt+Xr))|%}}.

steps.prompt: To find the fault currents for faults at each of 100 buses, $\mathbf Z_{bus}$ must be recomputed for every fault location.
steps.explanation: $\mathbf Z_{bus}$ depends only on the network, not on the fault location. Its diagonal holds every bus's Thévenin impedance, so a single matrix gives $I''_F = V_F/Z_{nn}$ for all buses, and its columns give the voltages during each fault.

steps.prompt: A generator ($X''_g$ = {{Xg}} pu) supplies a motor ($X''_m$ = {{Xm}} pu) through a link of {{XL}} pu. Before the fault the motor bus is at 1.0∠0° pu and the motor draws {{P}} pu at pf {{pf}} lagging. A bolted three-phase fault then occurs at the motor bus.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the fault current in per unit.
ask.explanation: Thévenin at the motor bus: $X_{th} = (X''_g + X_L)\parallel X''_m$ = {{Xa}} ∥ {{Xm}} = {{Xth||4}} pu. $I''_F = V_F/X_{th}$ = 1/{{Xth||4}} = {{IF|pu}}, purely inductive ($-j$); the prefault load current does not change it.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the generator current during the fault, in per unit.
ask.explanation: Prefault current $I_L = \mathbf S^*/\mathbf V^*$ = {{P}} − j{{Q}} pu. The fault-only part divides between the two sides: the generator side ($X_a = X''_g + X_L$ = {{Xa}}) carries $I''_F X''_m/(X_a + X''_m) = 1/X_a$ = −j{{1/Xa||4}} pu. Superposition: $I_g$ = {{P}} − j({{Q}} + {{1/Xa||4}}), so $|I_g|$ = {{sqrt(P^2 + (Q + 1/Xa)^2)|pu}}.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the motor's current during the fault (flowing into the fault), in per unit.
ask.explanation: The motor side carries the rest of the fault-only current: $I''_F X_a/(X_a + X''_m) = 1/X''_m$ = −j{{1/Xm||4}} pu. The prefault current {{P}} − j{{Q}} flowed **into** the motor, so it subtracts: $I_m$ = −{{P}} − j({{1/Xm||4}} − {{Q}}), $|I_m|$ = {{sqrt(P^2 + (1/Xm - Q)^2)|pu}}. Check: $I_g + I_m$ = −j{{IF||4}} = $I''_F$.

steps.prompt: A radial system: generator ($X''$ = j{{Xg}} pu) at bus 1, line 1–2 of j{{X12}} pu, line 2–3 of j{{X23}} pu. A bolted three-phase fault occurs at bus 3 ($V_F$ = 1.0 pu). Using $Z_{bus}$, find the voltage at bus 2 during the fault.
steps.explanation: For this radial network $Z_{33} = X''_g + X_{12} + X_{23}$ = {{Xg + X12 + X23}} and $Z_{23}$ = {{Xg + X12}} (the impedance common to the paths of buses 2 and 3 to the reference). $E_2 = 1 - Z_{23}/Z_{33}$ = {{1 - (Xg + X12)/(Xg + X12 + X23)|pu}}, the same as the divider $X_{23}/Z_{33}$.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a three-phase fault study in order.
items: Draw the per-unit reactance diagram with subtransient machine reactances
Find the Thévenin impedance at the fault bus (or $Z_{nn}$)
Split the fault current into the branches and add prefault currents if required
Convert to kA with the current base of each zone
steps.explanation: The network model comes first, then the Thévenin impedance at the fault, the total fault current, its distribution, and finally the conversion to amperes zone by zone.

steps.prompt: A 13.8-kV bus has a fault level of {{Ssc|VA}}. What series reactance (in ohms) must be inserted to limit the three-phase fault current to {{Imax|A}}?
steps.explanation: Needed total: $Z = V/(\sqrt3 I)$ = 13.8 kV/(1.732 × {{Imax|A}}) = {{13.8e3/(sqrt(3)*Imax)|Ω}}. Existing: $V^2/S_{sc}$ = {{13.8e3^2/Ssc|Ω}}. Reactor: {{13.8e3/(sqrt(3)*Imax) - 13.8e3^2/Ssc|Ω}} (reactances add, as both are nearly purely inductive).

steps.prompt: Why must breakers close to large generators cope with more asymmetry than those deep in the distribution network?
options: The X/R ratio is high there, so the DC offset decays slowly
Generators produce a DC voltage during faults
The fault current there is purely resistive
The subtransient reactance is larger than the transient reactance
steps.explanation: Generators and large transformers have very high $X/R$ (40 or more), so the DC time constant $T = (X/R)/\omega$ is long and much offset remains when the contacts part. In distribution networks lines and cables add resistance, $X/R$ is low and the offset dies out within a cycle or two.

steps.prompt: A fault with $X/R$ = {{XR}} has a symmetrical current of {{Isym|A}}. Find the rms asymmetrical current (maximum offset) {{tau}} cycles after fault inception.
steps.explanation: $K = \sqrt{1 + 2e^{-4\pi\tau/(X/R)}}$ = {{sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))||3}}, so the asymmetrical current is {{Isym*sqrt(1 + 2*exp(-4*pi*tau/XR))|A}}. At τ = 0 the factor would be √3 = 1.73, the theoretical maximum.
